input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

Describe the datasets per domain: internal author notes and, where available, a small curated set of PDFs. output:
We evaluate the proposed graph-aware prompting workflow on two topical domains selected to exercise different retrieval and citation characteristics: (1) a domain grounded primarily in internal author notes and project documentation, and (2) a domain supplemented by a small, manually curated set of published PDFs where available. These two domains were chosen to (a) reflect practical writing scenarios in which authors combine private notes and public literature, and (b) test the system's ability to integrate evidence from heterogeneous source collections during section-level generation.

Dataset composition and provenance. Each domain's source material comprises two kinds of inputs: internal notes (drafts, bullet-point summaries, and private technical memos produced by the authoring team) and, where available, a curated set of external PDFs (published papers and reports) intended to supply corroborating evidence. The internal notes are not publicly shareable for contractual and privacy reasons; the curated PDF sets are small and were assembled under standard access and licensing constraints. Because the internal materials are private, we do not report exact document counts or release raw source files; instead, evaluation focuses on citation fidelity and unsupported-assertion rates measured against the accessible evidence in each domain.

Preprocessing. Prior to retrieval and prompting, source documents are converted to plain text and partitioned into retrievalable snippets aligned to logical unit boundaries (paragraphs, figure captions, and section fragments). (General background knowledge: standard preprocessing steps include PDF text extraction or OCR when necessary, normalization of whitespace and encoding, and extraction of simple bibliographic metadata when present.) Snippets are indexed with provenance metadata (source identifier, snippet offset, and inferred section label) to enable per-section evidence injection and later traceability.

Data splits and evaluation protocol. To assess section-level generation under realistic constraints, we avoid large-scale trainable splits and instead adopt an evaluation protocol centered on generation-time retrieval and per-section auditing. (General background knowledge: for experiments that compare generation pipelines across a small curated corpus, common protocols include leave-one-document-out or document-level holdout; in this work we apply document-holdout strategies where feasible and report per-section metrics aggregated across held-out documents.) All generation and retrieval steps operate solely on the held-in sources for a given run; no model fine-tuning on the evaluation data was performed.

Privacy, licensing, and reproducibility. The use of internal author notes imposes reproduction constraints: raw source artifacts cannot be publicly released. Where permitted, we will release synthetic examples and anonymized snippets that reproduce the structural properties of the datasets (section granularity, citation density) without exposing private content. The curated PDF subsets are described in metadata tables (document-level identifiers, topical tags, and access restrictions) within the supplementary material; direct redistribution of full texts is contingent on publisher permissions. We discuss these reproducibility limitations and potential mitigations (e.g., shared public corpora and benchmark tasks) in the Limitations section.

Summary. The experimental domains therefore provide a pragmatic testbed for evaluating how graph-aware, leaf-first section scheduling and evidence-aware prompting affect citation coverage and unsupported-assertion rates when source evidence is heterogeneous and partially private. Detailed dataset statistics, example provenance records, and preprocessing scripts will be documented in the supplementary material to the extent allowed by data-sharing constraints.
